911.title: Bodhidharma
911.hook: the legendary Indian monk Chan remembers at its beginning, sitting with his face to a wall
911.howItsDone: In Soto Zen meditation halls in Japan, practitioners sit facing the wall, and Chan and Zen temples honor Bodhidharma's image as the first ancestor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four Chinese schools, Tiantai, Huayan, Chan and Pure Land. Your line: four Chinese schools. Today, Chan, at the place it says it began.

A blank wall. Rough plaster, a crack running down one corner. In front of it, a monk sits with his back to the room. Visitors come and go behind him. He doesn't turn around. In paintings he's drawn with a thick beard, heavy brows and wide, unblinking eyes. In Japan he became a round red doll with no arms or legs, weighted at the bottom, so every time you knock it over it rocks back upright. This is Bodhidharma, the monk Chan remembers at its beginning in China.
screen: `A MONK FACING A WALL.` → `BEARD, BROWS, WIDE EYES.` → `A DOLL THAT ROCKS BACK UP.`

segments.voice: First, who he was, as far as anyone can say. Tradition says he was a monk from India, some accounts say from the south and from a royal family, who came to China to teach. Beyond that, little about him is certain, and the stories grew longer and more colorful in the retelling. So it's honest to call him legendary: a real memory, wrapped in a great deal of story. Second, facing the wall. The Chan stories say he settled at a monastery on Mount Song and sat facing a wall, for years, saying little. A short teaching attributed to him speaks of wall-gazing: settling the mind so it stands like a wall, unmoved, with no difference left between self and other. Whether the wall was a real wall, a picture of the mind, or both, the image stuck. Third, the first ancestor. Chan tells its history as a line of teachers handing the teaching to students, mind to mind. In that line, Bodhidharma is counted as the first ancestor in China, the link back to India. The next few days bring the emperor who didn't understand him and the student who did. Fourth, why a wall. A wall gives you nothing: no view, no story, nothing to scroll. What's left is whatever the mind brings. That's the point. The red doll in Japan carries the same idea in a lighter key: knocked over, it comes back up, the way attention comes back after it wanders.
screen: `A MONK FROM INDIA, MOSTLY LEGEND.` · `WALL-GAZING ON MOUNT SONG.` · `CHAN'S FIRST ANCESTOR IN CHINA.` · `A WALL GIVES YOU NOTHING.` · then, large: `FACING THE WALL.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn toward a plain wall, close enough to see it but not so close you strain, and let your eyes rest half open on one spot; if you can't, lower your gaze to the floor. When a thought appears, let it play against the wall like a shadow, and pass. When you notice you've drifted, come back, like the doll rocking upright.
Bodhidharma. The legendary monk from India whom Chan counts as its first ancestor in China, remembered sitting with his face to a wall.
Your line: facing the wall. Nothing to look at, and the mind shows up anyway. Day nine hundred eleven, done.

912.title: No merit
912.hook: an emperor lists his temples and asks what merit he has made; Bodhidharma says none
912.howItsDone: Making merit through giving and service is part of Buddhist life in many forms, and some Chan and Zen teachers retell the Emperor Wu story as a warning against keeping score.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bodhidharma, the legendary monk with his face to the wall. Your line: facing the wall.

Temples built. Sutras copied. Monks and nuns supported. Offerings given. That's the list an emperor brings, in the old Chan story, to the strange monk from India. The emperor is Wu of Liang, a ruler devoted to Buddhism, and he wants to know one thing: after all this, how much merit have I made? It's a fair question, the kind a person asks after years of doing good. And Bodhidharma's answer is short. No merit.

First, the emperor's list. Merit, in Buddhist teaching, is the good that comes from good actions, and Buddhist texts speak of making it by giving, by supporting monks and by building places to practice. The emperor was doing exactly that, so the answer stings. Second, how the Platform Sutra explains it. In that text a local official, puzzled by the story, asks the teacher Huineng what Bodhidharma meant. Huineng says the emperor's building and giving bring blessings, good fortune, and that's real. But merit in the deeper sense, he says, is something else: seeing your own true nature, and treating everyone with the same humble respect. It isn't stored up like grain in a barn. It's found inside, in how you see and how you act. Third, another telling. The Blue Cliff Record, a later book of Chan stories, opens with a different version of the meeting. There the emperor asks, what is the highest meaning of the holy truths? Bodhidharma answers: vast emptiness, nothing holy. The emperor asks, then who is standing in front of me? Bodhidharma says: I don't know. The emperor doesn't understand, and Bodhidharma leaves and crosses the river north. Fourth, what the story aims at. It doesn't say giving is foolish; Huineng says it brings blessings. It aims at the ledger, the quiet counting in the back of the mind. A kindness done while keeping score is still a kindness. The Chan question is what it would feel like with no scoreboard running at all.

Don't scold it; just see it, and let the number fade. Then rest with the breath, holding lightly the thought of a small good thing no one would ever know was you.

913.title: Bring me your mind
913.hook: Huike asks Bodhidharma to put his mind at peace; Bodhidharma says, bring it here
913.howItsDone: Chan and Zen students study the exchange between Bodhidharma and Huike as a koan, and meditation teachers in several traditions invite students to turn and look directly at the mind that worries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an emperor's list of good deeds, and Bodhidharma's short answer. Your line: a kindness with no scoreboard.

Snow is falling. A man stands outside a monastery, waiting. Inside, the monk he has come to see sits facing a wall and doesn't turn around. The man is Huike. He has come a long way with one trouble, the kind that follows a person from room to room. When at last he speaks, he doesn't ask a clever question. He says: my mind isn't at peace. Please, teacher, settle it for me.
screen: `SNOW, AND A MAN WAITING.` → `A MONK WHO WON'T TURN AROUND.` → `MY MIND ISN'T AT PEACE.`

segments.voice: First, the request. The Gateless Gate, a collection of Chan stories with short comments, tells this as one of its cases. Huike's words are simple enough for anyone to say at three in the morning: my mind is not at peace; please pacify it. Second, the answer. Bodhidharma doesn't offer advice or a technique. He says: bring me your mind, and I'll pacify it for you. Hand it over. Put it on the table. Third, the search. Huike looks, and says: I've searched for my mind, and I can't find it. Bodhidharma answers: there, I have pacified it for you. That's the whole exchange. Chan remembers Huike as the student who received Bodhidharma's teaching, the second ancestor in its line. Fourth, what happened in that search. Huike was asked to do something odd: not to fix his mind, but to find it. When you go looking for the anxious mind, you find things: a thought about tomorrow, a tight feeling in the chest, a picture of someone's face, a sentence repeating itself. But they keep moving. You can't pick the whole thing up and hand it to anyone. Some readers hear Bodhidharma saying the trouble was never a solid object; others hear a teacher simply turning a student around to look. Either way, the peace in the story doesn't come from a new answer. It comes from looking straight at the question.

segments.voice: Bring up one small worry, not the biggest one, and gently go looking for the mind that's worried: is it in the head, the chest, does it have a shape or an edge? Each time you find a thought, notice it's already moving, and look again. If the worry softens, let it; if not, keep looking with curiosity.

Your line: I can't find it. A worry looked at closely keeps on moving. That's day nine hundred thirteen.

914.title: The woodcutter
914.hook: Huineng, a poor woodcutter who can't read, hears the Diamond Sutra in the market and his mind opens
914.howItsDone: Chan and Zen communities honor Huineng as the Sixth Ancestor, and the Platform Sutra, his story and teaching, is read and taught in Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Vietnamese temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Huike went looking for his anxious mind. Your line: I can't find it.

A young man in a market in the far south of China has just been paid for a load of firewood and turns toward the door. Near it, a stranger is reciting a Buddhist text out loud, just saying it, the way someone hums at work. The young man stops. He can't read. And as he listens, the Platform Sutra says, his mind opens. Today, the woodcutter Chan would come to honor as its Sixth Ancestor.
screen: `A STRANGER RECITING A SUTRA.` → `FIREWOOD SOLD IN THE MARKET.` → `THE WOODCUTTER STOPS.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. His name was Huineng, and the Platform Sutra lets him tell his own story. His father died when he was young. He and his mother were poor, and he sold firewood in the market to keep them both. He couldn't read or write. Second, what he heard. The text the stranger was reciting was the Diamond Sutra, a teaching on letting go of fixed ideas, even fixed ideas about the Buddha. Huineng asked where he had learned it. The man said: on East Mountain, from the teacher Hongren, who tells everyone to keep this sutra. The Platform Sutra says Huineng made sure his mother was provided for, and then walked north to find him. Third, the first meeting. Hongren asks where he's from and what he wants. Huineng says he's from the far south, and he wants only one thing: to become a Buddha. Hongren tests him with an insult. You're from the south, a barbarian, he says. How could you become a Buddha? Huineng answers: people may be from the north or the south, but Buddha-nature has no north or south. Fourth, the threshing room. Hongren doesn't praise him. He sends him to the back of the monastery to split wood and pound rice, and there Huineng works, unnoticed. Notice where this story puts its turning point: not in a temple hall or a library, but in a market, between a sale and the door, through a stranger who probably never knew.

segments.voice: Choose a sentence you've heard so often you've stopped hearing it: a saying from your family, a line from a prayer, a phrase from a song. Say it silently and slowly, as if a stranger in a market had just said it, and stay a few breaths with whichever word stands out. If nothing opens, that's fine; you've listened.

915.title: Two verses on the wall
915.hook: the head monk writes that the mind is a mirror to be wiped; Huineng answers that there is no mirror stand
915.howItsDone: Chan and Zen students learn both verses, Shenxiu's and Huineng's, and teachers use them to talk about steady practice and the mind's original clarity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the woodcutter Huineng heard a sutra between a sale and the door. Your line: heard in the market.

Late at night, by lamplight, a monk walks down a corridor with a brush and ink. He writes a short verse on the wall and goes back to his room without signing it. In the morning the whole monastery is reading it. The teacher Hongren had set a test: write a verse that shows your understanding, and whoever truly understands will receive the robe and become the next teacher in the line. Everyone expected the head monk to win. This is his verse.
screen: `A VERSE WRITTEN AT NIGHT.` → `HONGREN'S TEST.` → `TWO VERSES ON THE WALL.`

segments.voice: First, the mirror to be wiped. The head monk was Shenxiu, a respected teacher in his own right. His verse, in the Platform Sutra, says roughly this: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind is like a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it clean, again and again, and don't let dust gather. It's a beautiful picture of practice: steady, patient care. Second, a verse he can't write. In the threshing room, Huineng hears a boy chanting Shenxiu's lines. He can't read, so he asks someone to read the wall to him, and then asks someone to write his own answer beside it. Third, no tree, no stand. Huineng's verse turns Shenxiu's around: awakening has no tree, the bright mirror has no stand. Here the versions of the Platform Sutra differ. The older one found at Dunhuang says Buddha-nature is always clean and pure; later versions say that from the beginning there is not a single thing. Both end with the same question: where could the dust land? Fourth, what the two pictures mean. Shenxiu describes the mind as something to keep polishing. Huineng says the clear nature was never dirty in the first place. That night Hongren calls Huineng in secret, gives him the robe, and sends him south. Later Chan writers told the story as gradual against sudden, and it comes to us from Huineng's side. But both verses are still read, and some readers find room for both in practice: some wiping, and some moments of seeing there was nothing to wipe.

segments.voice: If there's a mirror or a phone screen nearby, wipe it slowly and watch the smudges go: that's Shenxiu's patient, honest work. Then close your eyes and notice what's aware of the breath right now. Rest a few breaths with Huineng's question, where does dust land, without needing an answer.

916.title: The Chan monastery
916.hook: Mazu and Baizhang: work, meals and meditation shaped into one life
916.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen monasteries today, residents share daily work periods, often called samu in Japanese, alongside meditation and meals eaten together in a set form.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Huineng's verse on the wall, a mirror with no stand. Your line: where does dust land.

A wooden board is struck outside the meditation hall, and the monks file out. Not to chant this time. To the fields, with hoes and baskets. The cook is already at the stove, the youngest monks are hauling water, and somewhere among them, bent over a row of vegetables, is the abbot. In a Chan monastery, the stories say, nobody was too senior to dig. Two teachers stand behind this picture: Mazu, who shook his students awake, and his student Baizhang, who gave the community its shape.
screen: `THE BOARD IS STRUCK.` → `EVERYONE TO THE FIELDS.` → `THE ABBOT DIGS TOO.`

segments.voice: First, Mazu. He was a teacher in Huineng's line, remembered for blunt answers, shouts and sudden questions. In the Gateless Gate, a monk asks him what Buddha is, and Mazu answers: this very mind is Buddha. Not somewhere else, not later. This mind, the one asking. Second, Baizhang and the rules. Chan is remembered as a school of meditation, and you might expect a Chan monastery to do nothing but sit. Tradition credits Baizhang with shaping rules for Chan communities, and those rules put sitting inside a whole day: a hall for meditation, meals eaten together in order and in quiet, and shared work for everyone. Third, work, meals and sitting as one life. In that picture, digging the garden isn't time off from practice, and washing the bowls isn't a chore to rush through. The same attention that watches the breath in the hall watches the hoe in the soil. Fourth, water and firewood. A layman named Pang, who studied with Mazu, put it in a short verse. His supernatural powers and marvelous deeds, he said, were these: carrying water and hauling firewood. It's a joke, and it isn't. If this very mind is Buddha, as Mazu said, then it's this mind that carries the water. A modern day has its own version of Baizhang's fields: dishes, laundry, commuting, typing. The Chan monastery's claim is that none of it has to be wasted time.
screen: `MAZU: THIS VERY MIND IS BUDDHA.` · `BAIZHANG: RULES FOR A WHOLE DAY.` · `WORK, MEALS AND SITTING AS ONE LIFE.` · `CARRYING WATER, HAULING FIREWOOD.` · then, large: `WORK IS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Choose a chore you'll do today, dishes, folding clothes, sweeping, and walk through it slowly in your mind: the water's temperature, the weight of the cloth, the sound of the broom. Notice where the mind usually runs off to while you do it. Then come back to the breath, and let the chore wait for its moment.

917.title: The persecution of 845
917.hook: a Tang emperor closes the monasteries; the teachings that needed little come through
917.howItsDone: Chinese Buddhists remember the persecution under Emperor Wuzong as one of the hard turns in their history, and Chan and Pure Land communities often tell it as part of their own story of carrying the teaching through.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Baizhang, and a Chan monastery where work, meals and sitting made one life. Your line: work is practice.

Bells are being lowered from temple towers and carted off to be melted down. Bronze images follow them into the furnaces. Monks and nuns are told to take off their robes and go home as ordinary subjects. The gates are shut. This is China under the Tang emperor Wuzong, and a monk from Japan, far from home, is writing it all down in his diary while he tries to get himself and his books out of the country. When the buildings go, what's left?
screen: `BELLS GO TO THE FURNACE.` → `ROBES COME OFF.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?`

segments.voice: The official histories of the Tang dynasty date the harshest of Wuzong's decrees to 845. The court had come to see the monasteries as a drain: land, metal and people outside the tax rolls, serving a teaching from abroad. Wuzong himself favored Daoist masters. His decrees closed monasteries across the empire and sent monks and nuns back to lay life. The monk from Japan was Ennin, and his diary lets us see it from the road: monks forced into lay clothes, images stripped, foreign monks sent away. To get home, he put on ordinary clothes himself. The worst of it was short; the histories tell that Wuzong died soon after, and the next emperor eased the ban. But schools that leaned on great libraries, rich estates and the court's favor were badly shaken. A common way of telling the story is that two schools came through more easily. Chan, whose monks, like Baizhang's, worked their own fields and taught face to face. And Pure Land, whose practice could be carried in a single breath: the name of Amitabha Buddha, said by anyone, anywhere, with no building at all. Underneath is an old teaching of the Buddha: all conditioned things pass away. An empire can take bells, roofs and robes. It is much harder to confiscate a habit of sitting still, or a name a grandmother says over the stove. So a week that began with Bodhidharma facing a wall ends with stories saying the teaching did not live in the buildings.
screen: `AN EMPEROR'S DECREES.` · `ENNIN'S DIARY SAW IT.` · `WHAT NEEDED LITTLE CAME THROUGH.` · `ALL CONDITIONED THINGS PASS.` · then, large: `WHAT SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that came through a hard time and reached you: a recipe in someone's handwriting, a song a parent sang, an old building on your street, a habit you kept through a bad year. Notice what it needed in order to last, and what it turned out not to need. If you'd like, bow to it slightly, with your head or only in your mind.
